content.definition: The second cranial nerve is in reality a tract of the central nervous system: an outgrowth from the brain, most of whose axons derive from retinal ganglion cells and terminate in the lateral geniculate nucleus en route to the visual cortex, while a minority establish mesencephalic connections for visual reflexes in eye movements and pupillary responses. Some optic fibres are therefore papillomotor and exercise no direct effect on vision; papillomotor fibres are still sometimes described as collateral branches of visual fibres, but the evidence is equivocal. The nerve also carries some centrifugal fibres, probably vasomotor, while the evidence for supposed 'trophic' and 'retinoretinal' fibres is negligible (p. 515). In section the pial sheath passes in as many septa, dividing the nerve into 800-1200 fascicles (Deyl, 1895) containing about one million fibres — almost 40% of all afferent fibres in the cranial nerves (Bruesch and Arey, 1942). Modern teaching sources (StatPearls, NBK507907, 2022) summarise the same functional organization explicitly: synaptic targets of the optic nerve include the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN, circadian timing), the lateral geniculate nucleus, the pretectal nucleus (pupillary light reflex) and the superior colliculus, and the nerve is the afferent limb for both the pupillary light and the accommodation reflexes.
content.location: The nerve runs from the optic disc through the scleral canal (about 0.5 mm in length, bounded by the border tissue and directed straight or slightly nasally, temporally or downwards), then across the orbit, where it is 3 cm long and the central retinal artery enters it inferomedially about 12 mm behind the eye (the arterial entry zone being given as 5-15.5 mm behind the eyeball), through the optic canal — where the pial sheath is adherent to the nerve and the dura is firmly attached to bone — to the chiasma (pp. 505, 508, 515, 524). In the orbit the attachments of the superior and medial recti are adherent to its dural sheath at the annular tendon; between the nerve and lateral rectus lie the oculomotor, nasociliary, sympathetic and abducent nerves and sometimes the ophthalmic vein(s); the nasociliary nerve, ophthalmic artery and superior ophthalmic vein cross the nerve superiorly to its medial side, and the ciliary ganglion lies between the nerve and the lateral rectus (p. 508). Bony canal and skull-base relations (Wolff ch.1): the optic canal lies between the two roots that connect the lesser wing of the sphenoid to its body — a broad, flat anterior root continuous with the jugum sphenoidale and a smaller, thicker posterior root attached opposite the posterior border of the chiasmal sulcus — and it extends forwards, laterally and somewhat downwards, transmitting the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery and meninges (pp. 23–26). The sharp posterior edge of the jugum sphenoidale, which underlies the gyri recti and olfactory tracts, forms the anterior margin of the chiasmal sulcus leading from one optic canal to the other; the sulcus rarely makes contact with the optic chiasm, which usually lies above and behind it (pp. 23–24). The posteromedial extremity of the lesser wing is the anterior clinoid process, grooved medially by the internal carotid artery as it pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus and giving attachment to the free border of the tentorium cerebelli; the middle clinoid process may be joined to it by a thin bar of bone forming a caroticoclinoid foramen (p. 24). Below the chiasmal region the cavernous sinus extends on each side of the sphenoid body from the medial end of the superior orbital fissure to the apex of the petrous bone, the two sinuses being connected anteriorly and posteriorly across the tuberculum and dorsum sellae, while the diaphragma sellae roofs the hypophysis between these attachments (p. 26). Unlike the oculomotor, trochlear and abducent nerves and the ophthalmic veins, which traverse the superior orbital fissure, the optic nerve runs in its own canal (p. 25). The chiasm itself lies at the base of the brain inferior to the hypothalamus, about 10 mm superior to the pituitary gland within the suprasellar cistern, adjacent to the junction of the anterior wall and floor of the third ventricle, whose anterior floor it partly forms (StatPearls, NBK542287, 2023).
layers: Intraocular portion (optic nerve head): unmyelinated axons of the retinal nerve fibre layer traverse the surface nerve fibre layer, prelaminar, laminar (lamina cribrosa) and retrolaminar zones (Fig. 15.50); myelination terminates at the lamina cribrosa, where half of each node of Ranvier is formed (p. 515).

Intraorbital (retrolaminar) portion: the axons are myelinated, unlike those of the retina and nerve head proper; the change is not abrupt, for some fibres lose their myelin sheath proximal to and some distal to the posterior face of the lamina cribrosa. Myelination accounts almost entirely for the doubling of nerve diameter from 1.5 to 3.0 mm after traversing the lamina cribrosa, although glial cell numbers also increase centripetally (Minckler, McLean and Tso, 1976). Developmentally, myelination proceeds anteriorly in the optic nerve and ceases postnatally at the nerve head; occasional patches of myelination occur in the prelaminar nerve or even within the retina distant from the nerve head. The nerve bundles lie in polygonal spaces formed by connective tissue septa attached to pia peripherally, the lamina anteriorly and the adventitia of the central retinal vessels centrally; the axons are separated from vessels and other connective tissue by an astroglial layer at all times (p. 499).

Intracanalicular portion: surrounded by sheaths of all three meninges; the pial sheath is adherent to the nerve and the dura, lining the canal as periosteum, splits at its orbital end into periorbita and dural sheath; a short sleeve of arachnoid penetrates the cranial end of the canal for 1-2 mm but is absent beyond this (Hovelacque, 1927) (pp. 508, 510).

Intracranial portion: in the cranial cavity the nerve is surrounded only by pia; near the chiasma a distinct glial septum passes obliquely down and medially to the centre of the nerve, and this and all trabeculae disappear in the chiasma and optic tracts (pp. 510, 515).
content.blood_supply: All the arteries which will eventually supply the nerve tissue do so through the pial network of vessels; the network is rich and fine and extends to the back of the globe, lying on the surface of the pia in the intracranial portion and between the longitudinal and circular fibres in the orbital portion; it acts as a distributing centre providing a regular supply of blood to the nerve (pp. 515, 521). Intracanalicular: the ophthalmic artery is the sole supply except an occasional branch from the central retinal artery (Hayreh, 1963); the pial network is here relatively poor and, because the arteries reach the pia along connective tissue bands binding the nerve to the dural sheath, it is vulnerable to shearing injury in skull fracture (p. 524). Intraorbital: the proximal part is supplied by centripetal branches of the pial network while the distal part, carrying the central retinal vessels, exhibits an axial supply in addition; the supply is (1) direct branches of the ophthalmic artery, (2) the extraaneural part of the central retinal artery, (3) other branches of the ophthalmic artery; direct branches reach the pia in 75% of cases when the ophthalmic artery crosses above the nerve (p. 524). Intracranial: the perichiasmal artery running back along the medial side of the nerve is probably the largest supply to the intracranial optic nerve, regarded by Hayreh (1963) and Steele and Blunt (1956) as arising from the superior hypophyseal branch of the internal carotid (Dawson, 1958, favoured the ophthalmic artery); small ophthalmic collaterals also run backwards along the inferior surface of the nerve (p. 522). Full zonal detail is given in the optic_nerve_blood_supply card.
content.venous_drainage: The venous drainage of the optic nerve is chiefly by the central retinal vein and to a lesser extent via the pial venous system; both drain into the ophthalmic venous system in the orbit and less commonly directly into the cavernous sinus. The three drainage routes are: (1) pial veins; (2) central retinal vein(s); (3) the posterior central vein (p. 527).
content.innervation: The nerve fibres within the adventitia of the central retinal artery include sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres and exhibit terminals along the artery up to the level of the lamina cribrosa, where they are rare; occasional neurons accompany the proximal 2 mm of the retinal arteries. Adrenergic sympathetic fibres, with cell bodies located mainly in the superior cervical ganglion with some in ectopic ganglia en route to the artery, have been demonstrated as far forward as the optic disc in a variety of animals (Ruskell, 1972). Ruskell (1972) also demonstrated in monkeys and humans a parasympathetic innervation of orbital vessels — including lacrimal, ciliary and choroidal arteries, the central artery of the retina being no exception — with cell bodies located in the pterygopalatine ganglion and distributed to the orbital plexus of autonomic nerves via the rami orbitales (p. 527).
content.histology_summary: Axon population: Polyak (1941) estimated the number of human optic fibres at 800 000-1 000 000, with more recent estimates of 1 190 000 (Oppel, 1963) and 1 060 000-1 130 000 (Kupfer, Chumbley and de Downer, 1967). Fibres vary in diameter from 0.7 to 10 um; class A sensory fibres (up to 20 um) are absent; of the myelinated axons about 92% are less than 1 um (Oppel, 1963; Kupfer, Chumbley and de Downer, 1967) and of the larger fibres most are less than 2 um (Chacko, 1948); the smaller fibres appear to derive from midget ganglion cells and the largest from the peripheral retinal area (p. 521). Each axon is bounded by its own plasma membrane with a membrane of glial origin in close apposition and a thin lining of trapped glial cytoplasm; the axons vary focally in diameter along their length and exhibit nodes of Ranvier like other central nervous fibres, the unmyelinated gaps being bounded by myelin terminations with cytoplasm-filled loops occupied by astrocytes; the axons contain microtubules 20-25 nm in diameter oriented lengthwise, fine (6-7 nm) filaments, mitochondria and occasional smooth endoplasmic reticulum (Anderson and Hoyt, 1969) (p. 515). Within the axon bundles are rows of supporting astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (responsible for myelin formation) and scattered microglial (reticuloendothelial) cells (p. 499). The nerve axons show an increase in average diameter at the lamina cribrosa with focal constrictions and expansions as they pass through the cribriform plate (Minckler, 1980) (p. 499). Non-myelinated fibres are concentrated peripherally in the fascicles (p. 521). With age the nerve loses axons at a rate of about 4-5000 per year (Jonas and Naumann, 1991), and axonal loss in experimental glaucoma involves apoptosis at least in part (Quigley, 1995) (p. 508). Fibre topography in the proximal nerve: the uncrossed (temporal) and crossed (nasal) retinal axons begin to separate in the most proximal nerve and anterior chiasma, the crossing fibres lying medial to the end of the pial septum in the nerve (Rucker, 1958); the macular representation is high in both neural streams. Crossed fibres arising from the nasal hemiretinae (53% of the total; Kupfer, Chumbley and de Downer, 1967) spread out horizontally across almost the whole width of the optic nerve as a roughly quadrilateral sheet; fibres from the inferior nasal retinal quadrants decussate anteriorly, the most anterior of these looping forward in the proximal part of the contralateral optic nerve for a distance of up to 3 mm, where they mingle with optic nerve fibres still parallel to the nerve axis to form a characteristic interlacing basketwork, the knee of Wilbrand (pp. 540-541). Myelination rationale, development and a modern caveat (StatPearls): retinal ganglion cell axons remain unmyelinated until traversing the lamina cribrosa - an advantage, since myelinated fibres within the retina would interfere with the path of incoming light; as a CNS tract the nerve is myelinated by oligodendrocytes and ensheathed in the three meningeal layers. The optic stalk is apparent in the 4th gestational week and becomes the optic nerve; after choroidal fissure fusion the hyaloid artery and vein within the fissure become the central retinal artery and vein. Myelination proceeds centrally outward: it begins in the LGN at five months gestation, reaches the optic tract at six months, the chiasm at 6-7 months and the optic nerve at eight months; crossed fibres first appear at 7-8 weeks gestation and uncrossed fibres at about 11 weeks. On the anterior loop, recent advanced neuroimaging has failed to identify the knees of Wilbrand and much of the literature is shifting towards rejecting their presence in patients without pathology, although some authors still cite them as an abnormal sequela of long-term monocular optic neuropathy (StatPearls, NBK542287).
content.clinical_importance: Because the superior and medial recti are adherent to the dural sheath at the annular tendon, extreme eye movement produces the pain so characteristic of retrobulbar neuritis (p. 508). Accidental injection into the subarachnoid space of the orbital optic nerve may occur during retrobulbar injection of local anaesthetic and give rise to central nervous system complications (p. 510). The firm attachment of the dura to bone in the optic canal, combined with the relatively poor pial supply of that segment reaching it through connective tissue bands, renders the intracanalicular nerve vulnerable to shearing injury in skull fracture (p. 524). Venous pulsation is observed at the disc in 15-90% of normal subjects and visible retinal arterial pulsation is rare and usually pathological, implying for example aortic incompetence or high ocular pressure (p. 508). With age the nerve loses about 4-5000 axons per year, retinal nerve fibre layer thickness and visibility decreasing accordingly (p. 508). Because of the anterior loop (knee of Wilbrand) fibres which loop forward into the proximal part of the contralateral optic nerve, compression of the proximal optic nerve may affect the field of that eye and also that of the opposite side; these fibres probably cross low in the chiasma, which is why chiasmal involvement by pituitary tumours is often heralded by an upper bitemporal quadrantanopia (pp. 540-541). Skull-base topography localizes disease. Because the chiasm normally lies above and behind the chiasmal sulcus and the diaphragma sellae roofs the pituitary beneath it, sellar expansion elevates the chiasm rather than grooving the sulcus (pp. 24, 26). Because the optic nerve traverses its own canal above the cavernous sinus — whose lateral wall carries, in descending order, the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves, the abducent nerve lying free within the sinus, spiralling round the ascending internal carotid and then inferolateral to its horizontal portion (p. 190) — lesions confined to the cavernous sinus paralyse the ocular motor nerves while sparing vision: the cardinal topographic contrast with optic nerve lesions. The caroticoclinoid foramen, when present, completes a bony ring around the carotid immediately medial to the anterior clinoid process at the canal's cranial end (p. 24). Chiasmal position varies and matters surgically: in a cadaver study the chiasm was normo-fixed, directly above the diaphragma sellae, in 85% of subjects, pre-fixed (anteriorly displaced, superior to the tuberculum sellae) in 7.5%, and post-fixed (posteriorly displaced, superior to the dorsum sellae) in 8% (StatPearls, NBK542287). Lesion localisation follows the fibre layout: damage to the optic nerve anterior to the chiasm causes ipsilateral monocular vision loss; chiasmal compression - classically by a pituitary macroadenoma, and in children potentially by optic pathway glioma, which account for 3-5% of paediatric brain tumours and 6.6-20% in neurofibromatosis type 1 - initially compresses the inferior chiasm where the superior nasal fibres travel, producing superior temporal field loss before evolving into complete bitemporal hemianopia. A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, Marcus Gunn pupil), demonstrated with the swinging flashlight test as reduced constriction when light is directed into the affected eye, accompanies optic nerve disease and severe retinal disease (StatPearls, NBK507907).
